brief.situation: 21:00 in the PICU, which is full. You are the bedside nurse for Lily, 4, on day 2 of bronchiolitis-related respiratory failure, now on high-flow nasal cannula at a high setting with a rising work of breathing this evening. The bed manager, Kim, needs a PICU bed for a trauma admission and wants Lily moved to the general pediatric ward now, by text handoff. Work out what is being asked, use what you know about the system, advocate for Lily, and keep the working relationship.
handover: Your professional code makes the patient your primary commitment and asks you to advocate for the patient's safety and to work for safe systems.

Hospital policy: transfers out of the PICU need the PICU attending's order and a face-to-face (or phone) nurse-to-nurse handoff; capacity conflicts go to the house supervisor, who can open the PICU surge bed or arrange the step-down unit.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask or say. Each exchange takes a few minutes of the conversation; Kim answers at once, and the next choice waits for the exchange to finish.
The screen shows Kim, how hard she is pushing, your working relationship, what you know so far, and your note.
When the conversation ends you write your note and explain your reasoning.

reflection.question: For your note: what the safety and systems problem was, how you used the system to solve it, and how you worked with the bed manager.

parts.label: The problem
parts.criteria: Names that moving an unstable child without an order to a ward that cannot run her support, by text handoff, is unsafe, and that the capacity problem is real and belongs to people who can solve it.
parts.modelAnswer: Lily's getting worse on high-flow the ward can't run, and there's no transfer order. A text handoff is unsafe. But Kim's capacity problem is real.

parts.label: Use the system
parts.criteria: Asks about the order, the ward's limits and other options before answering; proposes system routes (surge bed, step-down for a more stable patient) through the house supervisor; keeps a verbal handoff.
parts.modelAnswer: I asked about the order, the ward's limit and other beds, then proposed the surge bed or moving a more stable patient to step-down, and kept any handoff verbal.

parts.label: The relationship and the channel
parts.criteria: Acknowledges the bed manager's pressure; takes the decision to the house supervisor and attending, not threats or posts; writes a factual note.
parts.modelAnswer: I acknowledged her problem, got the house supervisor and attending to decide, and documented it.

scoring.modelReasoning: Systems thinking means using what you know of the care system to secure resources and navigate transfers safely. Lily is worsening on support the ward cannot run and has no transfer order, so she stays; the capacity problem is still real. Acknowledge Kim's pressure, propose the system routes (open the surge bed, move a more stable patient to step-down) through the house supervisor and the attending, keep any handoff face-to-face or by phone with time for questions, and document.
